title: Harmonizing standards and resources for the medical genome.
journal: Nature 655:47-58, July 2026 (PMID 42387168; PMC13506173, NIH author manuscript; Europe PMC isOpenAccess = N)

verified.what_i_actually_checked: There is nothing to open, and I checked that four ways. (1) Europe PMC search on the DOI returned exactly 1 hit with hasSuppl = 'N' and dbCrossReferenceList = null, i.e. no supplementary files and no database cross-references. (2) Europe PMC's fullTextXML endpoint returned HTTP 500, so I pulled the full text instead from NCBI as the NIH author manuscript (efetch db=pmc id=PMC13506173, HTTP 200, 160,484 bytes, manuscript ID NIHMS2194319) and parsed it myself: 25 section titles, 2 narrative tables, 2 figures, zero <supplementary-material> elements, zero <media> elements, zero occurrences of the string 'data availab', zero occurrences of 'Extended Data'. (3) NCBI elink from PubMed 42387168 to GEO DataSets, SRA, BioProject, BioSample, dbVar, ClinVar and dbGaP returned an empty linkset for every one of the seven databases. (4) Zenodo application programming interface search on the DOI returned 0 records; a Figshare title search returned only unrelated articles. The only web addresses in the whole article text are organization home pages (NIST genome-editing consortium, Human Genome Structural Variation Consortium, ClinGen, NIH SMaHT, FDA and EMA guidance pages, a BioRender figure credit).
verified.what_came_from_paper_text_only: Everything about the content. This is a Perspective-style consensus article from Ashley, Doudna and 26 co-authors that reviews genome data quality standards for four clinical contexts (germline sequencing, tumour sequencing, cell-free DNA testing, and sequencing as quality control for genetic therapies) and issues recommendations. I read its text, including the passage citing a 34% variant-calling accuracy improvement from pangenome alignment relative to Genome in a Bottle (GIAB, a United States National Institute of Standards and Technology benchmarking consortium) reference materials - but that number is a citation to prior work, not data deposited with this paper. The two tables are lists of consortia and of technical standards, written as prose cells, not measurement tables.

a1_downloadable.note: FAILS, and in the most basic way: the paper has no dataset at all. It is a standards and recommendations Perspective with no new measurements, no supplementary files (Europe PMC hasSuppl = 'N', zero supplementary-material elements in the PubMed Central full text), no accession numbers, no data availability statement, and no deposit in Zenodo, Figshare or Dryad. All seven NCBI elink queries from the PubMed record came back empty. This is not a controlled-access problem that an application could fix; there is nothing to request.

a2_label_is_a_column.note: Not applicable. No table of measurements exists, so there is no column of any kind. The quantities the paper discusses (precision, recall and their harmonic mean F1 for variant calls; limits of detection for low-frequency variants) are described in prose, not tabulated.

a3_inputs_present.note: Not applicable. No inputs are deposited. The resources the article points to (GIAB benchmark materials, the Human Pangenome Reference Consortium assemblies) are third-party resources that exist independently of this paper and are raw sequencing reads and assemblies, which my project rules forbid downloading.

a4_units_stated.note: Not applicable; no data file, so no units column. The article itself is careful about terminology and includes a definitions-and-abbreviations box, but that is editorial, not a data dictionary.

a5_enough_rows.note: Zero data rows. The only tabular objects in the article are two narrative tables: one listing consortia that advance genomic quality standards, one listing technical standards across clinical applications. Both have on the order of ten rows of free text.

a6_fits_laptop.working_set: 0 bytes of the paper's own data; the 160,484-byte full-text XML is all that downloads
a6_fits_laptop.note: Trivially fits, and trivially useless. Any real project built on this article's themes would have to start from GIAB or pangenome sequencing data, which is terabyte-scale and excluded by the project's size filter and no-raw-sequencing rule.

a7_counts_match_paper.note: Nothing to compare. The paper states no counts of its own data because it has none; the numbers it quotes are citations to other publications.

a8_label_provenance.note: Not applicable. Worth noting for any future attempt in this area, though: GIAB 'truth' variant call sets, which this field treats as ground truth, are themselves consensus calls built by combining many callers across platforms, so a model trained to match them is partly learning a consensus procedure rather than a direct physical measurement.

existing_models.name: DeepVariant (Google), a deep neural network that calls genetic variants from sequencing reads
existing_models.score_and_split: Won the 2016 precisionFDA Truth Challenge for best single-nucleotide-variant performance and the 2020 Truth Challenge V2 in the all-benchmark-regions categories for Oxford Nanopore, PacBio and multi-technology entries; those challenges are run by the United States Food and Drug Administration with the Genome in a Bottle consortium on held-out benchmark genomes. Taken from a web search summary of the project page and challenge results, not from a paper I retrieved in full.
existing_models.authors_named_unsolved: Not established by me; I did not retrieve the DeepVariant papers' discussion sections, because the evaluation had already stopped at the A1 failure.

existing_models.name: Clair3, a deep-learning small-variant caller for long reads
existing_models.score_and_split: Reported median F1 (harmonic mean of precision and recall) of 99.99% for single-nucleotide variants and 99.53% for insertions/deletions, on benchmark-genome evaluations; roughly 2 million model parameters against DeepVariant's roughly 20 million. From the same web search summary, not from a full-text retrieval.
existing_models.authors_named_unsolved: Not established by me, for the same reason.

c2_audit.note: This is a partial audit, done only to characterize the field around the nearest conceivable project (machine learning on medical-genome benchmark data). It is enough to show the field is crowded with open, reproducible, independently benchmarked models, which would make C2 = 0 even if data existed. I did not pursue the full five-part audit because the evaluation stopped at the A1 failure.

backbone.name: None applicable. A deoxyribonucleic-acid (DNA) language model such as AlphaGenome or DNABERT-2 would be the generic choice for medical-genome tasks, but there is no data here to attach a head to.
backbone.licence: The article itself is an NIH author manuscript in PubMed Central with no open licence statement ('available for text mining', reprints via Nature); irrelevant since there is no data to license.

integration.partner_dataset: None. The named third-party resources (Genome in a Bottle benchmark materials, Human Pangenome Reference Consortium assemblies, ClinGen) are all joinable to each other, but this paper contributes no table to join them to.
integration.bigger_question_one_sentence: Not assessed: stopped at A1, and a join needs at least one dataset on our side.

honest_claim_h3: Not assessed: stopped at A1. No model can be trained from this article, so there is no claim to state.

plain_idea.one_liner: Use benchmark sequencing data to predict which parts of the human genome stay hard to read accurately.
plain_idea.train_on: This was the project I considered and could not build: one row per genomic region, with features describing the local DNA (repeat content, how similar nearby sequence is, how many copies of a gene exist) and, as the measured outcome, how well standard pipelines call variants there. Number of examples: unknown, because the paper deposits no such table - the counts would have to come from third-party benchmark resources.
plain_idea.predict: The accuracy of variant detection in a region, measured as precision, recall and their harmonic mean (F1) against a consensus benchmark call set. Those benchmark call sets are produced by the Genome in a Bottle consortium by combining multiple sequencing platforms and callers on a small number of well-studied human cell lines.
plain_idea.why_worthwhile: Clinical laboratories and the groups writing genome quality standards would use a map of which medically important genes remain unreliable, to decide where a second confirmatory assay is required. Nothing in this paper supports building that map, so the idea would have to start from the benchmark consortia's own releases instead.

ml_idea: No viable machine-learning project comes from this paper. It is a recommendations document: its output is a set of proposed standards for genome data quality across germline, tumour, cell-free DNA and gene-therapy sequencing, not a dataset. If the topic is interesting, the route in is the Genome in a Bottle and Human Pangenome Reference Consortium releases directly - but those are raw and assembled sequencing data at terabyte scale, excluded by this project's size and no-raw-sequencing rules, and the prediction task closest to them (variant calling) is already served by open, independently benchmarked models.

effort.compute_note: Nothing to estimate. The only thing that downloaded was the 160,484-byte full-text XML, which parsed in under a second. All other numbers are null because no dataset exists.
effort.cheapest_killing_check: Already run, in about two minutes: Europe PMC reports hasSuppl = 'N' and no database cross-references for this DOI, the PubMed Central full text contains zero supplementary-material elements and no data availability statement, and NCBI elink from the PubMed identifier to GEO, SRA, BioProject, BioSample, dbVar, ClinVar and dbGaP returns empty for all seven.

verdict_reason: A1 fails: the paper is a standards-and-recommendations Perspective with no data of its own - no supplementary files, no accessions, no data availability statement, no repository deposit. Its two tables are prose lists of consortia and standards. The nearest real project would require terabyte-scale benchmark sequencing data that my rules exclude, in a task already covered by open, independently benchmarked variant callers.
